title: Cancer Pain Management: Multimodal, Multidisciplinary Strategies
summary: A multimodal, interprofessional approach combines pharmacologic therapy (anchored by the WHO ladder), nonpharmacologic therapies, interventional techniques, and psychosocial care to achieve superior analgesia, reduce opioid exposure, and improve function and quality of life. Evidence supports combining cognitive-behavioral therapies and other non-pharmacologic approaches with drug therapy, and leveraging structured multimodal analgesia perioperatively for cancer surgery.
clinicalQuestion: In adults with cancer-related pain, what multimodal strategies optimize analgesia, minimize opioid burden, and improve function and quality of life?

heroStats.label: CBT + Pharmacotherapy vs Drug Alone
heroStats.value: Greater pain reduction; pooled effects favor combination therapy [3]

heroStats.label: Perioperative MMA in Head & Neck Cancer
heroStats.value: Lower opioid use (OMEs) with similar/better pain control [6]

heroStats.label: Care Model
heroStats.value: Multidisciplinary, interprofessional adoption growing in US [1]

keyMoments.title: Anchor to the WHO Analgesic Ladder, modernized
keyMoments.body: Start with non-opioids, escalate to weak/strong opioids as needed, and integrate adjuvants early for neuropathic or bone pain while continuously reassessing goals and toxicities [7].

keyMoments.title: Combine pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic therapies
keyMoments.body: Adding CBT and other nonpharmacologic therapies to drug therapy yields superior analgesia and functional outcomes versus drugs alone in cancer-related pain [3].

keyMoments.title: Perioperative multimodal analgesia (MMA) reduces opioid exposure
keyMoments.body: Structured MMA pathways in cancer surgery (e.g., head and neck) reduce opioid consumption with maintained or improved pain control, supporting opioid stewardship [6].

keyMoments.title: Interprofessional care is essential
keyMoments.body: Integrated teams (oncology, palliative care, anesthesia pain, rehab, psychology) are increasingly used across US systems to implement multimodal, multidisciplinary pain care [1], [8].

keyMoments.title: Tailor to pain mechanism
keyMoments.body: Differentiate nociceptive, neuropathic, visceral, and bone pain; match adjuvants and interventions accordingly to maximize benefit and limit adverse effects [7].

sections.title: Stepwise Multimodal Strategy
sections.blurb: Integrate pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic modalities with continuous reassessment, aligned with patient goals and disease trajectory.

steps.title: Assess mechanism, intensity, and impact
steps.body: Characterize pain type (nociceptive, neuropathic, bone, visceral), severity, temporal pattern, functional impairment, psychological distress, and risk factors for opioid-related harm. Screen for breakthrough and incidental pain, and document prior responses.

steps.title: Initiate WHO ladder–based pharmacotherapy with adjuvants
steps.body: Begin with acetaminophen and NSAIDs if safe; escalate to weak then strong opioids for moderate–severe pain while adding adjuvants early for neuropathic (gabapentinoids, SNRIs, TCAs) or bone pain (bisphosphonates, denosumab) and corticosteroids when indicated. Reassess frequently to optimize balance of analgesia and adverse effects [7].

steps.title: Embed nonpharmacologic therapies
steps.body: Offer CBT, mindfulness-based interventions, exercise/physical therapy, and other evidence-based modalities alongside pharmacotherapy; combination approaches **improve pain outcomes beyond drugs alone** in cancer-related pain [3].

steps.title: Use procedural/interventional options when focal or refractory
steps.body: Consider regional anesthesia, neuraxial techniques, nerve blocks, vertebral augmentation, or neurolytic procedures for localized pain or when systemic therapy is limited by toxicity; perioperative multimodal pathways reduce opioid use while preserving analgesia in cancer surgeries [6].

steps.title: Implement interprofessional care and opioid stewardship
steps.body: Coordinate with oncology, palliative care, pain specialists, rehab, and behavioral health. Standardize bowel regimens, antiemetics, naloxone co-prescribing when risk is elevated, and taper plans as disease and treatment change. US systems are increasingly adopting multimodal, multidisciplinary programs [1], [8].

sections.title: Practical Multimodal Options by Mechanism and Setting
sections.blurb: Combine modalities to enhance efficacy and minimize toxicity; monitor for cumulative adverse effects.

cards.title: Core Pharmacologic Toolkit (WHO Ladder)
items: Non-opioids: acetaminophen; NSAIDs if platelet/renal/GI risk acceptable [7]
Opioids: titrate short-acting to effect; convert to long-acting with rescue for breakthrough; monitor sedation/constipation/nausea [7]
Neuropathic pain adjuvants: gabapentin/pregabalin; duloxetine/venlafaxine; TCAs (anticholinergic caution) [7]
Bone pain: bisphosphonates or denosumab; consider corticosteroids for capsular/edema-related pain [7]
Visceral/colicky pain: antispasmodics; consider celiac/splanchnic block for upper abdominal malignancy pain when refractory [7]

cards.title: Nonpharmacologic Therapies (combine with drugs)
items: Cognitive-behavioral therapy and mindfulness: **additive pain reduction vs pharmacotherapy alone** in cancer pain [3]
Physical therapy/exercise and pacing; manual therapies as adjuncts [3]
Acupuncture and relaxation-based techniques where available [3]
Education, goal setting, and self-management skills; caregiver training [3]

cards.title: Perioperative Multimodal Analgesia (Cancer Surgery)
items: Regional anesthesia and nerve blocks; local anesthetic infiltration [2], [6]
Scheduled acetaminophen/NSAIDs unless contraindicated; gabapentinoids with caution [2], [6]
Opioid-sparing adjuncts (ketamine, dexmedetomidine) per protocol [2]
Structured pathways in head & neck cancer surgery: **reduced OMEs with maintained or improved pain control** [6]

cards.title: Opioid Stewardship and Safety
items: Set functional goals; use lowest effective dose; avoid rapid escalation [7]
Prophylaxis: stimulant laxatives ± softener; antiemetics as needed [7]
Assess risk (sleep apnea, renal/hepatic impairment, concurrent sedatives); consider naloxone when risk high [7]
Monitor for hyperalgesia, cognitive effects; plan taper during remission or after procedures [7]

cards.title: When to Escalate/Refer
items: Uncontrolled pain despite optimized multimodal therapy
Suspected neuropathic or plexus involvement needing interventional evaluation
High toxicity burden limiting systemic options
Complex psychosocial distress requiring specialized behavioral interventions [1], [8]

cards.title: Follow-up and Reassessment
items: Frequent early reassessment (24–72 hours after changes); adjust for effect and adverse events
Document pain intensity, function, sleep, mood, and breakthrough episodes
Revisit goals-of-care and deprescribe when possible; maintain bowel and antiemetic plans
Integrate survivorship and end-of-life needs across the trajectory [7]

sections.title: Head & Neck Cancer and Complex Surgical Cases
sections.blurb: High nociceptive and neuropathic burden; airway and swallowing issues complicate analgesia.

steps.title: Enhanced recovery-aligned MMA
steps.body: In major head and neck oncologic surgery, **MMA reduces opioid consumption** (OMEs) with similar or better pain scores; consider scheduled non-opioids, regional techniques, and cautious gabapentinoid use to limit sedation/respiratory risk [6].

steps.title: Functional targets
steps.body: Prioritize swallowing, communication, and mobilization milestones; involve speech and physical therapy early to align analgesia with rehabilitation goals [5], [6].
